name: St Mary Magdalene's Church, Creswell
text: Your train passes near St Mary Magdalene's Church in Creswell, on the train's {side}, built in 1899 and 1900 as the gift of the 6th Duke of Portland, to designs by Louis Ambler. Its tower followed in 1927, with a ring of eight bells from John Taylor of Loughborough.

name: Worksop Town F.C.
text: Your train passes near the home of Worksop Town Football Club, the Tigers, on the train's {side}. In the FA Cup in 1923 the club held Tottenham Hotspur to a goalless draw at White Hart Lane, before losing the replay there.

name: Steetley Colliery
text: Your train passes near the site of Steetley Colliery, on the train's {side}, on the border of Derbyshire and Nottinghamshire, where miners reached coal in December 1875. It was linked underground to Whitwell Colliery in 1894 to ventilate both pits, and its surface works closed in 1983 when it was joined to Shireoaks.

name: Mr Straw's House
text: Your train passes near Mr Straw's House, on the train's {side}, an Edwardian semi-detached house of about 1905 that the Straw family hardly changed after the 1920s. When the grocer's son William Straw died in 1990, he left it to the National Trust with some 30,000 everyday objects, and it opened to the public in 1993.

name: Worksop Priory
text: Your train passes near Worksop Priory, on the train's {side}, an Augustinian priory founded by William de Lovetot in 1103. When it was dissolved in 1539, its property went to the Earl of Shrewsbury on condition that he provide a glove for the sovereign's right hand at the coronation, a custom still kept today.

name: Newark flat crossing
text: Your train crosses the Nottingham to Lincoln line on the level at the Newark flat crossing, the last place on Network Rail where two standard gauge lines cross like this. It is renewed about every 16 years, most recently in August 2019.

name: Gainsborough Old Hall
text: Your train passes near Gainsborough Old Hall, on the train's {side}, built by Sir Thomas Burgh in 1460 and one of the best preserved medieval manor houses in England. Burgh entertained Richard III there in 1484, and Henry VIII visited Gainsborough twice.

name: West Burton power stations
text: Your train passes near the West Burton power stations, on the train's {side}, beside the River Trent. West Burton A, a coal-fired station opened in 1966 on the site of the deserted medieval village of West Burton, stopped generating on March 31st 2023, and its site is planned for the first fusion power plant of the STEP programme.

name: Battle of Gainsborough
text: Your train passes near the scene of the Battle of Gainsborough, on the train's {side}, fought on July 28th 1643 in the First English Civil War. The Parliamentarians foiled a Royalist attempt to retake the town, and Colonel Oliver Cromwell made his name there as a cavalry leader.

name: Lincoln Racecourse
text: Your train passes near the old Lincoln Racecourse on the Carholme, on the train's {side}, where James I acted as clerk of the course in 1607. It was the first home of the Lincolnshire Handicap, which moved to Doncaster after the course closed in 1964; its grandstand of 1897 is listed.

name: Tunman Wood
text: Your train passes near Tunman Wood, on the train's {side}, ancient woodland of more than 53 hectares that has stood since at least 1774. The Forestry Commission used it from the 1940s, and in 2009 the county and district councils and Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust bought it as a local nature reserve.

name: Collingham F.C. (Nottinghamshire)
text: Your train passes near Station Road, home of Collingham Football Club, on the train's {side}. The club was founded in 1887, and in 2001 it played in the FA Vase for the first time, reaching the first round proper.

name: Winthorpe Bridge
text: Your train passes near Winthorpe Bridge, on the train's {side}, a concrete box girder bridge carrying the A1 over the River Trent. It was built by the Danish firm Christiani & Nielsen, opened by Ernest Marples on July 27th 1964, and is listed Grade II*.

name: Newark Castle
text: Your train passes near Newark Castle, on the train's {side}, founded in the mid 12th century by Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln. King John died there in October 1216, by tradition after a surfeit of peaches, and the castle was slighted after the English Civil War.

name: Southwell Racecourse
text: Your train passes near Southwell Racecourse, on the train's {side}, one of only six racecourses in the UK with an all-weather track. The jockey Hayley Turner grew up locally and had her first job in racing with a trainer beside the course.

name: St Denis' Church, Morton
text: Your train passes near St Denis' Church in Morton, on the train's {side}, a parish church built in 1756 and listed Grade II*. It shares a parish with the churches at Rolleston and Upton.

name: Thurgarton railway station
text: Thurgarton station, at one end of this stretch, is listed Grade II. It stands on the Nottingham to Lincoln line, engineered by George Stephenson and opened by the Midland Railway on August 3rd 1846, and much of its original decoration remains.

name: St Laurence's Church, Gonalston
text: Your train passes near St Laurence's Church in Gonalston, on the train's {side}, a church dating from the 14th century that Thomas Chambers Hine rebuilt in 1843.

name: St Helen's Church, Burton Joyce
text: Your train passes near St Helen's Church in Burton Joyce, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church built in the 13th century. Its south aisle was added in 1725, and T. H. Wyatt rebuilt the arcades in 1878.

name: Carlton Town F.C.
text: Your train passes near the home of Carlton Town Football Club, the Millers, on the train's {side}. The club was founded in 1904 as Sneinton Football Club, and in 1909 the Manchester Courier called it the leading amateur football club in Nottingham.

name: St Mary's Church, Nottingham
text: Your train passes near St Mary's in the Lace Market, on the train's {side}, the oldest parish church in Nottingham and one of only five Grade I listed buildings in the city.

name: Meadow Lane
text: Your train passes near Meadow Lane, on the train's {side}, home since 1910 of Notts County, the oldest professional football club in the world. Nottingham Forest's City Ground is just 300 yards away across the River Trent: the two are the closest pair of football grounds in England.

name: Rectory Junction Viaduct
text: Your train crosses the River Trent on Rectory Junction Viaduct, built in 1850 with a cast iron arch of 110 feet, as the Trent Navigation Company demanded a clear span of at least 100 feet. Its timber approach viaduct was rebuilt in brick in 1909 and 1910.

name: Saxondale, Nottinghamshire
text: Your train passes near Saxondale, on the train's {side}, a hamlet where 30 people lived at the 2021 census. A branch line once left the railway here at Saxondale Junction and ran through Bingham to Melton Mowbray, and traces of it can still be seen.

name: Church of St Mary and All Saints, Bingham
text: Your train passes near the Church of St Mary and All Saints in Bingham, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed medieval church restored by George Gilbert Scott in 1845 and 1846. Its tower holds eight bells: two were added to the ring of six in 1922.

name: Cranmer's Mound
text: Your train passes near Cranmer's Mound, on the train's {side}, the motte of Aslockton's 12th-century castle, about 16 feet high. It bears the name of Thomas Cranmer, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1533 to 1553, who was born in the village.

name: St Mary the Virgin's Church, Bottesford
text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin's Church in Bottesford, on the train's {side}, whose chancel was rebuilt in the 17th century to hold the monuments of the Manners family, earls and later dukes of Rutland. One of their tombs is famous for an inscription that blames two of the family's deaths on witchcraft by the Witches of Belvoir.

name: Church of St Lawrence, Sedgebrook
text: Your train passes near St Lawrence's Church in Sedgebrook, on the train's {side}, the village's only Grade I listed building. It is largely of the 15th century, with an early 13th-century north arcade and a 14th-century chancel arch.

name: Francis Trigge Chained Library
text: Your train passes near St Wulfram's Church in Grantham, on the train's {side}, where Francis Trigge set up a chained library in 1598 in the room over the south porch. It was the first library in England endowed for use outside an institution such as a school or college.

name: St Bartholomew's Church, Langford
text: Your train passes near St Bartholomew's Church at Langford, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church dating from the 13th century. The River Trent once flowed beside it, until a great flood in 1575 changed the river's course.

name: Grantham Guildhall
text: Your train passes near Grantham Guildhall, on the train's {side}, completed in 1869 to designs by William Watkins. The statue of Sir Isaac Newton by William Theed in front of it is older: it was put up in 1858, when a school stood on the site.

name: Newbo Abbey
text: Your train passes near the site of Newbo Abbey, on the train's {side}, a house of Premonstratensian canons founded in about 1198 near Sedgebrook. It was suppressed in 1536; stone coffins dug up there in about 1920, one of them an abbot's, are now at Belvoir Castle.

name: Church of St Mary, Wilsford
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church in Wilsford, on the train's {side}, a Grade I listed church which, with its tower and spire, dates from the 11th to the 15th centuries. All its fittings are from the 19th century except the 15th-century octagonal font.

name: Sleaford Castle
text: Your train passes near the site of Sleaford Castle, on the train's {side}, built between 1123 and 1139 by Alexander, Bishop of Lincoln. King John and Henry VIII both stayed there; it fell into disrepair in the late 16th century.

name: Cogglesford Mill
text: Your train passes near Cogglesford Mill, on the train's {side}, a working watermill on the River Slea. There is evidence of a Saxon mill on the site; the present brick building dates from the 18th century, and stoneground flour is still milled and sold there.

name: Car Dyke
text: Your train passes near Car Dyke, on the train's {side}, a ditch running for more than 57 miles along the western edge of the Fens. It is generally accepted as Roman work, and its northern section is by far the longest artificial waterway the Romans built in Britain.

name: Bass Maltings, Sleaford
text: Your train passes the Bass Maltings, on the train's {side}, eight malt houses built for the Bass brewery between 1901 and 1907, the largest group of malt houses in England. They closed in 1959, and a fire in 1976 badly damaged three of them.

name: Heckington Windmill
text: Your train passes Heckington Windmill, on the train's {side}, the only eight-sailed tower windmill still standing in the United Kingdom with its sails intact. Built in 1830 for Michael Hare, it was known as the Station Mill for its closeness to Heckington station.

name: Hubberts Bridge
text: Your train passes near Hubberts Bridge, on the train's {side}, a village named after its bridge over the South Forty-Foot Drain. The first bridge was of wood, as was its replacement of about 1850; a brick bridge designed by John Kingston, the county surveyor, followed in 1888.
